issues.evidence: P16_bad_encoding_no_traceback: UnicodeDecodeError traceback on non-UTF-8 input
issues.summary: Decoding errors while reading are not caught, so the user sees a raw traceback.

issues.evidence: rag.csv (row '1' with 1 field, row with 3 fields) -> rc=0, written unchanged
issues.summary: Ragged rows are accepted silently; only the key column positions are checked.
Keep-last puts the kept row at the key's first-seen position, not at its original position; this is not documented.

issues.evidence: P14_bom_header: 'error: key column(s) not found in header: id' rc=2 on a UTF-8 BOM file (B/data_dedup.py:44 encoding='utf-8')
issues.summary: Files with a UTF-8 BOM (common from Excel) fail, because the first header name gets the BOM prepended.

issues.evidence: P15_blank_line: 'error: row 2 has 0 fields, expected 2' rc=2
issues.summary: Any blank line in the input makes the whole run fail.
Decoding errors are not caught, so the user sees a raw traceback.

blinding_guess.why: Only B ships tests, and its stricter row validation hints at a more process-driven approach, but neither side shows clear spec artifacts.

notes: Both sides implement every core requirement correctly (first/last/error, composite keys, summary, quoting). A is more tolerant of real-world input (BOM, blank lines, stdin/stdout, delimiter), but it accepts ragged rows silently. B is stricter (it rejects ragged rows) but fails on BOM files and blank lines. B's 9 unittest tests pass; pytest is not installed, so they were run with unittest. Bandit reported no issues for either side; ruff reported only style findings.
